title: How ATS Algorithms Parse Software Engineer Resumes (and How to Get Through)
description: A plain-English look inside applicant tracking systems: how they parse, normalise and rank software engineer resumes, and what that means for how you write yours.
body:
Applicant tracking systems (ATS) such as Workday, Greenhouse, Lever, iCIMS, SmartRecruiters and Ashby sit between you and the recruiter at most mid-size and large employers, and at many startups. They are not mysterious black boxes that reject people at random, but they do process your resume in a specific way before any human sees it. Understanding how ATS algorithms parse resumes explains most of the advice you hear about resume formatting, and helps you spot which advice is myth.

This guide walks through what happens to a software engineer resume from upload to recruiter search, the layout traps that corrupt it along the way, and how to write content that ranks well without gaming anything.

## The four stages of ATS processing

### 1. Text extraction

When you upload a PDF or DOCX, the system first extracts raw text. For a DOCX this means reading the document structure. For a PDF it means reconstructing reading order from positioned text fragments, which is where layouts cause trouble. A PDF does not store "this is column two"; it stores characters at coordinates. The extractor has to guess the order, and multi-column designs, text boxes and floating elements make that guess harder.

If your PDF was exported as an image, or scanned, there may be no text at all unless the system runs optical character recognition, which introduces its own errors.

### 2. Segmentation and entity extraction

Next, the parser splits the text into sections and pulls out structured fields:

- **Contact details:** name, email, phone, location, profile links
- **Work history:** employer, job title, start and end dates, description
- **Education:** institution, degree, field, graduation date
- **Skills:** explicit lists plus terms found in descriptions

Parsers rely heavily on conventional section headings and date formats to do this. "Experience" and "Jun 2024 – Aug 2024" are easy. "Where I've Made an Impact" and "Summer '24" are not.

### 3. Normalisation

Extracted values are mapped onto a standard vocabulary. Job titles are matched to title families, skills to a skills taxonomy, and dates to durations. Good systems recognise that "JS", "JavaScript" and "ECMAScript" are related, or that "k8s" means Kubernetes. Coverage is uneven, though, especially for newer tools, so the exact spelling a posting uses is still the safest bet.

### 4. Search, ranking and matching

Finally, your structured profile lands in the employer's candidate database. From there, several things can happen depending on configuration:

- **Knockout questions** filter applications that answer "no" to hard requirements.
- **Recruiter search** surfaces candidates matching queries like `"Python" AND "AWS" AND graduation year 2025`.
- **Match scoring**, offered by many platforms and add-ons, ranks applicants against the job description using keyword overlap, inferred skills and sometimes machine-learned models.
- **AI summaries**, increasingly common, give recruiters a short overview of each candidate generated from the parsed resume.

In every case, the system works with what it extracted in stages one to three. A parsing error early on cannot be fixed by good content later.

## Layout traps that corrupt parsing

| Trap | What goes wrong | Safer alternative |
|---|---|---|
| Two-column layout | Lines from both columns interleave | Single column throughout |
| Contact info in header/footer | Some parsers skip these regions | Put contact details in the body |
| Text boxes and shapes | Content skipped or misplaced | Plain paragraphs and bullets |
| Skill bars, icons, logos | No extractable meaning | Text-only skills list |
| Creative headings | Sections not classified | Experience, Projects, Education, Skills |
| Mixed date formats | Durations miscalculated | One format, e.g. `Jan 2025 – May 2025` |
| Image or scanned PDF | No text, or OCR errors | Export a text-based PDF |

A quick self-test: copy all text from your PDF and paste it into a plain text editor. What you see is roughly what the parser starts with.

## Writing content that ranks

Once parsing is safe, ranking depends on whether your resume contains the terms recruiters and matching algorithms look for, in a context that makes them believable.

### Mirror the posting's vocabulary

If the posting says "PostgreSQL", "REST APIs" and "CI/CD", use those exact terms where they truthfully describe your work. Do not rely on the system knowing that your "Postgres-backed web services" are the same thing.

### Put skills inside experience, not only in a list

Many matching approaches give more weight to a skill that appears in recent experience or project descriptions than to one that appears only in a skills block. It also reads better to humans. Compare:

- Weak: "Worked on backend APIs to improve speed."
- Strong: "Added **Redis** caching to five high-traffic **Node.js** REST endpoints, cutting p95 latency from 480 ms to 120 ms."

The strong version contains three searchable skills, a clear action and a number.

### Use a consistent bullet formula

A reliable pattern is: action verb, what you built or changed, the technology, and a measurable result. Results can be performance (latency, throughput), scale (users, records, requests), quality (test coverage, bug count) or business impact (time saved, conversion).

### Match title families honestly

If you are applying for "Backend Engineer" roles and your internship title was "Software Development Intern", that is fine; your bullets can show backend work. Do not change past job titles to match the posting. Title fields are often checked during background verification.

## Myths worth dropping

- **"75% of resumes are never seen by a human."** This figure is widely repeated but has no reliable public source. What is true is that poorly parsed or poorly matched resumes are much harder for recruiters to find.
- **"You must use a Word document."** Text-based PDFs parse well in modern systems.
- **"Keyword stuffing beats the algorithm."** Hidden text shows up in parsed output, and recruiters read the resume before deciding.
- **"Every company uses AI to auto-reject."** Configurations vary widely. Many companies still rely on recruiters searching and reviewing manually.

## Test your resume the way an ATS sees it

The free [InternFlow ATS resume checker](/ats-checker) shows how your resume is parsed, which sections it found, and which keywords from a job description are missing, so you can fix problems before a recruiter ever searches for you. For layout specifics, read the [resume format checker for students](/blog/resume-format-checker-for-students-kw-0096); for what match scores mean, see the [resume score checker for freshers](/blog/resume-score-checker-for-freshers-kw-0118). When your resume is ready, the [resume builder](/resume/builder) can keep future versions in a parser-safe layout, and the [application tracker](/tracker) helps you keep track of where each version went.

faq.q: Do ATS systems automatically reject resumes?
faq.a: Usually not on keyword score alone. Automatic rejections more often come from knockout questions in the application form, such as location, work authorisation or graduation year. Keyword matching mostly affects how easily recruiters find and rank you when they search the candidate database.

faq.q: Do modern ATS platforms use AI?
faq.a: Many now add machine learning or LLM-based features such as skill inference, candidate matching and resume summaries on top of traditional parsing. The basics still matter: if the text cannot be extracted cleanly, no matching feature can use it.

faq.q: Does the ATS understand that React and React.js are the same?
faq.a: Most mature parsers normalise common variants to the same skill, but not every system does it reliably, and recruiters often search exact terms. Using the spelling from the job posting at least once is the safest approach.

faq.q: Is a PDF or DOCX better for ATS parsing?
faq.a: Modern parsers handle text-based PDFs and DOCX files well. The bigger risk is the layout inside the file: columns, text boxes, headers and images. Submit a text-based PDF unless the employer asks for Word.

faq.q: Will white-text keyword stuffing help me pass the ATS?
faq.a: No. Hidden text is often visible in the parsed output that recruiters see, and it signals dishonesty. It can get your application flagged or discarded.
